item.title: Quantum copper steals the show at LME Week
item.description: The guest of honour at the London Metal Exchange (LME) Week was Doctor Copper, who spent last week defying the laws of physics, or at least London transport, by managing to be at every seminar, cocktail party and private meeting.
item.dc:creator: Andy Home
item.content:encoded: The guest of honour at the [USN:L8N4620UG TEXT:"London Metal Exchange (LME) Week"] was Doctor Copper, who spent last week defying the laws of physics, or at least London transport, by managing to be at every seminar, cocktail party and private meeting. Maybe there were two of them at the annual gathering. Was Doctor Copper's US double in attendance? After all, there are two very distinct copper markets right now. Perhaps Doctor Copper was also using an AI-generated hologram, given the market's fortunes seem increasingly tied to the massive global investment in next-generation data centres. Despite copper being the hot topic of just about every conversation last week, no one seems any the wiser as to where the red metal , currently holding near record highs above $14,000 per metric ton, is headed. This is because copper, ever the bellwether of global manufacturing, encapsulates the new metallic order, one in which demand, to quote Saad Rahim, chief economist at trade house Trafigura, is "everything, everywhere all at once," but supply is fragmented by government policy. QUANTUM COPPER Copper remains the bull pick of the LME metals pack thanks to a compelling narrative of stellar demand prospects and structurally challenged supply. Around three-quarters of those attending the LME Seminar on Monday picked it as the top performer over the next 12 months, although the share dropped to around half when the LME remembered it also trades tin and included the soldering metal in the follow-up poll. But is the copper market currently oversupplied or undersupplied? The answer is both, depending on where you are. At a global level, there is no shortage. The International Copper Study Group now expects a global supply surplus of 104,000 metric tons this year and a larger one of 368,000 tons next year. Global exchange inventory is over 1.2 million tons, double year-ago levels. But all the metal is sitting in the US thanks to the [USN:L8N45V0YV TEXT:"continued uncertainty"] as to whether President Donald Trump will impose import tariffs. Everyone else is short of metal, [USN:L4N45F0JN TEXT:"particularly China"], where Shanghai Futures Exchange inventory amounts to just 54,400 tons and the closely watched Yangshan import premium has surged to a 13-year high of $168 per ton over the LME price. The Chinese copper market is currently the "tightest I've seen it in my career", Nicholas Snowdon, head of research at commodity trader Mercuria, told the Financial Times Metals and Mining Summit. The global copper market has fractured, and so too has pricing. "The reality is that one price fits all isn't effective," according to Jin Hennig , global head of metals at CME Group (CME.O) , which is rapidly listing new storage capacity to handle the flood of metal washing up in the US. Copper has truly entered a quantum state, where reality depends on where you are observing the market. POLICY RULES, OK? It's not just copper that is increasingly beholden to government policy. Aluminium's regional fragmentation, manifest in wildly divergent physical premiums, is also down to Trump's 50% import tariffs. Might Canada, traditionally the largest supplier of metal to the US market, get a [USN:L8N44N1RM TEXT:"tariff discount"]? The mood music between the White House and the Canadian government doesn't hold much promise, but according to Jorge Vazquez, founder of Harbor Aluminum, the chances of a tariff reset on Canadian metal are as high as 75%. If it were to happen, US premiums would collapse and European premiums could almost double to over $1,000 per ton over the LME cash price, Vazquez told the LME Seminar. Meanwhile, nickel's short-term price prospects are totally dependent on what happens next [USN:L8N45E0RC TEXT:"in Indonesia"], which over the last decade has grown to become the world's dominant producer. "The outlook now depends less on the scale of announced capacity and more on whether Indonesian policy continues to limit ore availability and prevents a return to persistent oversupply," according to Nikhil Shah, head of nickel analysis at research house CRU. Want to make sense of the cobalt market? You need to be tracking government policy in the [USN:L8N42V0NT TEXT:"Democratic Republic of Congo"], the world's largest supplier of the battery metal. Those export controls are propping up the price but at the cost of a massive accumulation of in-country stocks, described by CRU's Thomas Matthews as "a Pandora's box" of uncertainty. As metals become ever more strategic, government policy becomes ever more embedded in traditional supply-demand analysis. Which is why everyone last week was talking about Doctor Copper. Or should that be Doctors Copper? (The opinions expressed here are those of Andy Home , a columnist for Reuters.) Enjoying this column? Check out Reuters Open Interest (ROI), your essential new source for global financial commentary. Follow ROI on LinkedIn, and X. And listen to the Morning Bid daily podcast on Apple , Spotify , or the Reuters app . Subscribe to hear Reuters journalists discuss the biggest news in markets and finance seven days a week.

item.title: Instant View: Anthropic IPO filing to put AI investment boom to the test
item.description: Anthropic made its US IPO filing public on Monday, edging toward what could be the first stock market debut by a frontier AI lab and laying out the promise, costs and risks of building AI meant to transform the global economy.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Anthropic made its [USN:L3N46C10M TEXT:"US IPO filing"] public on Monday, edging toward what could be the first stock market debut by a frontier AI lab and laying out the promise, costs and risks of building AI meant to transform the global economy. The IPO comes at a time when market volatility has thinned the fall listing calendar and rising borrowing costs have sharpened investor concerns over the debt-fueled AI investment boom. Wall Street's main indexes were higher in morning trade with the S&P 500 (.SPX) up 0.5%. U.S. stock index futures got a brief boost after the IPO filing. COMMENTS: JOSH STEVENS, CHIEF INVESTMENT OFFICER, CRESALTA INVESTMENT MANAGEMENT, COLORADO "I'm optimistic about AI as a technology. And Anthropic is certainly exciting. But are we going to rush in and buy at the IPO? No. Even great ideas or business models end up seeing their share prices come down to attractive levels during times when investors are reassessing demand and supply. And then, you've got an opportunity to go in and buy." PETER ANDERSEN, FOUNDER OF ANDERSEN CAPITAL MANAGEMENT, BOSTON "I think it's a significant milestone in the development of artificial intelligence. And the outcome of this IPO will be fairly indicative of the sentiment for continuing to support capital expenditures in the development of artificial intelligence." THOMAS HAYES, CHAIRMAN, GREAT HILL CAPITAL, NEW YORK "In the general sense of a business doing $16 or $32 billion annualized revenue, and losing $80 to $160 billion a year, a $1.5 trillion valuation seems rich. The offering is for the faithful, that sooner or later, they're going to get some return on that invested capital. The price could go up because they'll control the supply of stock that they issued, but in the long term, it's a weighing machine and losing that amount of money on that investment until they turn the corner, which is many years out, you'll have better places to buy it than at the initial public offering." "If people are raising cash for the Anthropic IPO with funds from the current hyperscalers in Mag Seven, that could be a headwind in coming weeks. It will be dependent on what we see in earnings from Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon this week." BRIAN MULBERRY, CHIEF MARKET STRATEGIST, ZACKS INVESTMENT MANAGEMENT, COLORADO"It'll be very interesting because Meta has come out and said we're going to raise another $95 billion in an equity offering as well, so you're going to have really a saturated market. There's a lot of liquidity that needs to get scooped up by these two offerings at the same time. I think it could be a detrimental to some of these smaller and maybe even lower quality AI names that are out there." LUKAS MUEHLBAUER, ASSOCIATE AT IPOX SCHUSTER, EDINBURGH "Anthropic’s IPO will certainly establish a benchmark for valuing leading AI labs, influencing both upcoming listings and confidence in the companies funding the AI infrastructure buildout." "Its success would not necessarily benefit every AI business equally, as investors will still distinguish between proven customer demand and spending based on anticipated growth." ANDRE BAKHOS, MANAGING MEMBER, INGENIUM ANALYTICS LLC IN PLAINSBORO, NEW JERSEY "It speaks a lot that the AI trade is alive and well. That the penetration of AI will continue. It also bolsters the psychology looking at the other participants in this space." "It's a race for capital and it's telling that there is growth. But also there are going to be questions coming in regarding valuations, regarding how long can this go for." ROBERT PAVLIK, SENIOR PORTFOLIO MANAGER, DAKOTA WEALTH IN FAIRFIELD, CONNECTICUT "It's a challenging environment, to say the least, exactly when this IPO will take place. There's a lot riding on not only the company, but the AI industry." "If it goes well, that could help return investors confidence to the AI industry. But it's going to be challenging." "Maybe the environment changes after the (US midterm) elections next week. You're going to have to make major promises that I don't know if they can be fulfilled anytime soon." MATT KENNEDY, SENIOR STRATEGIST AT RENAISSANCE CAPITAL "Investors weren't questioning valuations the same way a few months ago. With some of the hottest AI IPOs of the summer trading below their offer price, not even Anthropic will get a blank check." "Maybe they could have gotten a higher valuation next year, but they've decided to 'rip the band-aid off'." "For Anthropic, being publicly traded is also of strategic interest: This is a PBC (Public Benefit Corporation), and being publicly traded provides a greater level of public transparency."

item.title: Anthropic's IPO: A close look at AI frontrunner's rapid growth, spiraling costs
item.description: Anthropic unveiled its US initial public offering paperwork on Monday, setting up for a blockbuster market debut that would test investors' willingness to fund the AI juggernaut's bills amid growing worries over the massive debt-fueled spending.
item.dc:creator: Deborah Sophia
item.content:encoded: Anthropic [USN:L3N46C10M TEXT:"unveiled"] its US initial public offering paperwork on Monday, setting up for a blockbuster market debut that would test investors' willingness to fund the AI juggernaut's bills amid growing worries over the massive debt-fueled spending. The company had submitted a [USN:L4N4291D9 TEXT:"confidential filing"] in June. In the recent weeks, exclusive reporting from Reuters highlighted its [USN:L6N45L00I TEXT:"sweeping AI ambitions"], [USN:L4N4500J8 TEXT:"mounting costs"] and concerns about the "[USN:L4N45K1J5 TEXT:"existential risks to humanity"]" that advanced AI poses. Here are a few details on Anthropic's financials, business structure, and where it stands in the global AI race: BACKGROUND AND FINANCES Founded in 2021 by former OpenAI researchers including siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, Anthropic is the startup behind the Claude family of AI models. Across four tiers - Fable, Opus, Sonnet and Haiku - Claude powers products such as Anthropic's chatbot, coding agent and the enterprise-focused Claude Cowork AI agent. Anthropic's early focus on training its models for coding tasks propelled the company to the forefront of the AI race and helped it draw a steady stream of enterprise customers. A majority of its revenue comes from businesses paying for its models per use, measured in "tokens" of information processed, in what Anthropic calls "consumption-based" revenue. It also generates revenue from its paid customer subscription tiers such as "Pro" and "Max". That has helped Anthropic grow its revenue to $4.59 billion in 2025 from $386 million a year ago and $41 million in 2023. For the six months ended June 2026, Anthropic's revenue was $16.29 billion, a massive increase from $1.16 billion for the same period in 2025. The company's operating losses have ballooned over the past years. But for the first half of 2026, they stood at $693 million, narrowing from $2.14 billion in the first half of 2025, as a fourteen-fold jump in revenue offset a fivefold increase in overall expenses. COSTS, COMPUTE DEMAND AND CIRCULAR AI INVESTMENTS Computing power is Anthropic's biggest expense. The company's costs include computing fees paid to cloud services providers such as Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud, costs tied to data center facilities and renting data center capacity, equipment leases and energy bills. Over the past three years, Anthropic's compute and infrastructure expenses have dwarfed its revenue. The company has committed more than [USN:L1N45K0RM TEXT:"$600 billion"] in spending with about eight partners over a decade - one of the largest AI buildout commitments on record. Anthropic said many portions of its agreements are non-cancelable or require payments regardless of usage. It has committed to spend at least $110 billion with Amazon (AMZN.O) , about $114.5 billion with Google (GOOGL.O) and $44.9 billion with Microsoft for cloud computing over the next seven to 10 years. But some of those companies are also its largest backers. Amazon and Google are among Anthropic's top shareholders, marking yet another example of the circular financing structures that have dominated capital flows in the AI industry. Amazon has invested at least $13 billion in Anthropic and has agreed to invest up to $20 billion more. Google has committed up to $40 billion to Anthropic. GOVERNANCE AND STRUCTURE Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, or PBC, meaning it is legally obligated to balance profitability goals for investors with developing AI for the benefit of humanity. An independent body elects a majority of its board. The company, helmed by Dario Amodei as CEO and his sister Daniela, as president and chair of the board, will continue to operate as a PBC after its listing. It expects to keep its founders and an independent trust in control, in a structure that could limit investor oversight and public shareholders' influence. The company has said it needs to concentrate control and capital in fewer hands to reduce AI's risks. Under this arrangement, a majority vote of its seven co-founders will direct a single share of Class F stock that amounts to 50.1% of the total voting power over key corporate matters, including the election of some board directors and other matters submitted to investors. COMPETITION Anthropic's most direct competitor is OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, whose 2022 launch kick-started the global race to adopt and advance AI technologies. Following Anthropic's lead in the enterprise market, OpenAI has sharpened its focus on products for developers and business customers. Anthropic is also locked in a race with Elon Musk's SpaceX, Alphabet's Google and Meta (META.O) . All of them are spending billions of dollars into model development, data centers and specialized AI chips as they vie for dominance in generative AI. Ramp data, which captures a slice of AI spending by business customers, showed Anthropic accounted for 60.1% of AI token spending in the week ended October 11.

item.title: From Amazon to Google, the deep-pocketed investors in Anthropic
item.description: Only a few startups have attracted as much investor conviction as Anthropic. Backed by some of the biggest names in technology and finance, the AI company has seen its valuation soar through successive funding rounds.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Only a few startups have attracted as much investor conviction as Anthropic. Backed by some of the biggest names in technology and finance, the AI company has seen its valuation soar through successive funding rounds. Its [USN:L3N46C10M TEXT:"initial public offering"] now offers a closely watched test of whether investors beyond Silicon Valley share that enthusiasm for the leaders of the AI boom. Here's a look at the key investors backing the Claude maker: Investor Details Amazon Amazon has invested at least $13 billion in Anthropic and in April agreed to invest up to an additional $20 billion. Anthropic also committed to spend more than $100 billion on the e-commerce giant's cloud services over 10 years Alphabet's Google Google has committed up to $40 billion to Anthropic, including an initial $10 billion investment announced in April. The partnership provides Anthropic with cloud infrastructure and access to Google's AI chips, which are used to train and run Claude models Spark Capital Spark Capital led Anthropic's $450 million Series C round in May 2023 and gained board representation through general partner Yasmin Razavi Lightspeed Venture Partners Lightspeed led the $3.5 billion Series E round in March 2025 and later co-led the $13 billion Series F round at a $183 billion valuation in September that year Fidelity Management & Research Fidelity participated in Series E and co-led the $13 billion Series F financing at a $183 billion valuation. The firm's other investments include Databricks and CoreWeave Salesforce Ventures Salesforce Ventures participated in the $450 million Series C round and the $3.5 billion Series E financing. The software firm's venture arm has also invested in firms such as Cohere and Chainguard ICONIQ Capital ICONIQ led the $13 billion Series F round at a $183 billion valuation and later co-led the $30 billion Series G financing. The venture capital firm's investments include OpenAI and smart ring maker Oura GIC Singapore's sovereign wealth fund led the $30 billion Series G round at a $380 billion valuation. GIC has also invested in AI voice generation startup ElevenLabs Coatue Management Coatue led the $30 billion Series G financing and later co-led the $65 billion Series H round. The investment firm has also financed companies such as Canva and CoreWeave D1 Capital Partners D1 Capital invested across multiple large financings including Series E, Series F, Series G and Series H. The firm has holdings in Cognition AI and SpaceX Sequoia Capital Sequoia was a significant investor in Series G and became one of the lead investors in the $65 billion Series H round at a $965 billion valuation Altimeter Capital Altimeter invested in the September 2025 $13 billion fundraise and was a lead investor in the $65 billion Series H financing at a $965 billion valuation Jaan Tallinn Skype co-founder Tallinn led Anthropic's first institutional financing, a $124 million Series A round in 2021. The angel investor has also funded open-source AI startup Zyphra and Rain AI Eric Schmidt The former Google chief executive has backed Anthropic personally and is among the company's best-known individual investors. Schmidt has also funded Yann LeCun's Advanced Machine Intelligence Menlo Ventures Menlo made its first investment in Anthropic in 2023 as part of a Series C round, and led Series D at an $18.4 billion valuation in 2024. It also participated in the $3.5 billion Series E round at a $61.5 billion valuation.

item.title: Egypt approves military support for Saudi Arabia after Houthi attacks escalate
item.description: Parliament authorised Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Monday to take "all necessary measures" to help Saudi Arabia defend itself — a move that could push Cairo more directly into the conflict between the kingdom and Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Parliament authorised Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Monday to take "all necessary measures" to help Saudi Arabia defend itself — a move that could push Cairo more directly into the conflict between the kingdom and Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis. Sisi had [USN:L6N46403J TEXT:"asked parliament"] to approve military support for Egypt's Gulf Arab ally and the world's biggest oil exporter if Riyadh requested help in fighting the Houthis, whose advances also threaten the strategic [USN:L8N4520BL TEXT:"Bab el-Mandeb Strait"] — southern gateway to the Red Sea and Egypt's Suez Canal. At least two-thirds of the chamber backed the measure, according to an official parliamentary statement. Parliament voted in closed session without publishing the tally, and no formal Saudi request for Egyptian troops has been announced. The statement did not specify what kind of support Egypt would provide. Taher al-Khouly, deputy head of parliament’s legislative committee, told Reuters that Egypt would send forces to Saudi Arabia in coordination between the two countries and at Saudi Arabia’s request. Several opposition groups opposed or declined to back the move. The Civil Democratic Movement, a coalition of opposition parties, rejected Egyptian military involvement in a regional war and said last week that Cairo’s role should focus on mediation. The Egyptian Social Democratic Party had said its lawmakers would abstain, citing a lack of information on the mission’s aims, duration and cost, while saying it remained supportive of Saudi Arabia. Egypt has frequently condemned Iranian and Iranian-backed attacks on Gulf countries, but it has not publicly engaged in direct combat or joined the Mecca [USN:L1N45R0S7 TEXT:"mutual defence"] pact between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey, [USN:L6N4440IT TEXT:"signed in August"]. Ministers from the pact’s member countries held an emergency meeting in Riyadh [USN:L1N45R0S7 TEXT:"earlier this month"] and agreed to ensure the “rapid deployment” of forces and military capabilities in Saudi Arabia. Pakistan approved the agreement last week, whileTurkey's parliament began ratifying it [USN:L6N4660OA TEXT:"last week"]. Top officials from the three Mecca pact countries were meeting Iranian leaders in Tehran on Monday in [USN:L2N46C041 TEXT:"a push to de-escalate the conflict"]. Britain said [USN:SPN46200R TEXT:"last week"] it would deploy Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets on missions to help protect Saudi cities and critical infrastructure from Houthi aerial attacks. SISI SPELLS OUT LIMITS OF EGYPTIAN SUPPORT FOR SAUDIS The Cairo parliament had postponed the vote last week as Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and intelligence chief Hassan Rashad travelled to Riyadh to deliver a letter to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman from Sisi, who said Egypt's support would be limited to defending Saudi territory and borders rather than attacking Yemen. Abdelatty said afterwards that Cairo advocated exploring [USN:L1N4680Z9 TEXT:""every opportunity""] to resolve the Yemen conflict diplomatically. Essam Farid, the speaker of the Senate, said Egypt’s position was "purely defensive" and aimed at defending Saudi territory, borders, sovereignty and holy sites against external attack. He said that it would not extend to an attack on Yemen and that Egypt stands with its brothers as "a shield that protects, not a sword that attacks". Egypt, the Arab world's most populous state with one of the region's largest militaries, joined the Saudi-led coalition in an earlier phase of Yemen's war, in March 2015. At that time it acted mainly as a naval partner, sending warships to secure Red Sea shipping lanes. It also deployed around 800 ground troops but played only a limited combat role. Egypt was involved in a costly military intervention in Yemen in the 1960s and has not undertaken a large-scale foreign ground deployment since the 1991 Gulf War. Yahya Ali al-Rai, speaker of Yemen's Houthi-run House of Representatives, last week urged the Cairo parliament to reject the proposal, saying Egypt would be threatening its own national security and internal stability. The Senate speaker told the chamber he had received a letter from Ahmed Obeid bin Daghr, head of Yemen’s Shura Council, which is aligned with the internationally recognised government, backing Egypt’s participation in defending Saudi Arabia. Bin Daghr said the position reflected the will of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, according to the speaker. Saudi Arabia is a major political and financial partner of Cairo, providing billions of dollars in aid, deposits at the central bank and energy supplies under Sisi. Fighting between the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognised government and the Houthi militia, which controls the capital Sanaa, has escalated in recent weeks, becoming a volatile front in the US-Israeli war on Iran . The Houthis have attacked [USN:L1N45W03M TEXT:"Riyadh's international airport"] and the state oil company [USN:L1N45Z0HH TEXT:"Saudi Aramco"], disrupting flights and oil exports, while aid agencies have warned of worsening conditions in Yemen, already suffering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises. The Saudi crown prince had sought military help from the US, but President Donald Trump did not agree to strikes on the Houthis, people familiar with the matter told Reuters in September. Washington told Riyadh that it would help with intelligence sharing and targeting, they added. (This story has been corrected to change the attribution of the remarks to Sisi, not the letter, in paragraph 13.)

item.title: Netanyahu touts Trump endorsement on eve of vote, suggests they may restart war on Iran
item.description: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu boasted of his endorsement from Donald Trump on the eve of Israel's election, suggesting the two leaders could restart their war against Iran if he wins.
item.dc:creator: Steven Scheer, Emily Rose
item.content:encoded: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu boasted of his endorsement from Donald Trump on the eve of Israel's election, suggesting the two leaders could restart their war against Iran if he wins, after Trump said they should "finish the job". "US President Donald Trump has come with a friendship that has never existed before between an Israeli prime minister and an American president. And it is doubtful we will ever have such a friendly president again," Netanyahu said in a televised appearance late on Sunday night. "He has another two years, and he says he is calling on you to vote for me." In his own social media post on Sunday, Trump, who launched the Iran war jointly with Netanyahu in February, said: "Vote for Bibi Netanyahu for Prime Minister, we have to finish the job that we started!" Netanyahu said Trump was willing to take action "that would finally, finally, remove the Iranian threat", but only as long as Netanyahu himself remains in power. "And I have already instructed the Mossad and the IDF (military) to bring down this regime, to bring down this regime because that is the only way to put an end to this threat," Netanyahu said, referring to Israel's main intelligence service and military. Asked for comment on Netanyahu's remarks, White House Deputy Press Secretary Anna Kelly said: “As President Trump stated, Iran is in very bad condition, both economically and militarily, and the blockade will remain in full force and effect, with oil flowing in record numbers of barrels through the Hormuz Strait." "The United States will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the [TOPIC:"reuters:/world/us/elections/" TEXT:"midterm elections"]," Kelly added via email, referring to the November 3 vote in the US. Trump first endorsed Netanyahu on October 18, reiterating his support in a post on Truth Social on Sunday. Asked by reporters later on Monday whether Netanyahu had requested the second endorsement, Trump said: "I never spoke about it." "I put out both endorsements. I put out both... I think he's done a very good job as prime minister under very trying conditions." Netanyahu's leading opponent, centrist former military Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, posted his own comments on social media, praising Trump as "a true friend of Israel". "I value his efforts and his commitment to Israel’s security, and I am confident that he will work in full cooperation with any leader chosen by the people." EISENKOT ACCUSES NETANYAHU OF FEAR-MONGERING Tuesday's vote, Israel's first since the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks, is the first chance for voters to deliver a [USN:L8N4680E4 TEXT:"verdict on the worst security failure"] in generations and the wars on multiple fronts that followed. With Netanyahu already at the helm of the most right-wing government in Israeli history, politics have shifted even further to the right. Nearly all Jewish-led parties, including that of the hawkish Eisenkot, now [USN:L6N4660BW TEXT:"oppose the "two-state solution" that underpinned decades of peace negotiations"] with the Palestinians. But many voters say the divisive politics of Israel's longest-serving leader make the country weaker. Polls suggest Netanyahu's Likud Party will lose seats, potentially depriving his coalition of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties of its narrow majority. Eisenkot and an array of opposition parties ranging from the rump of the centre-left to the right, also have no clear path to unseat him. Netanyahu, 77, is an unrivaled master of political survival: the only time since 2009 that opponents managed to wrest him briefly from the premiership, it took four inconclusive elections within two years to get him out. He was back 18 months later. Neither side planned major public events for Monday. But both posted on social media, drumming on the election's major themes — for Netanyahu, that he is the only leader with the mettle to face down Israel's enemies; for his opponents, that his divisive politics have weakened the country. Netanyahu shared an AI-generated video on Monday of Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, whose father Ali Khamenei was killed on the first night of US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February. Lying in a hospital bed, the younger Khamenei says his own vote would be "definitely not Bibi. Another term like this and I will be meeting my father sooner than expected." On Sunday Netanyahu posted a computer-generated photo of a mushroom cloud over Tel Aviv, saying Israel was in existential danger from Iran. [USN:L6N46303T TEXT:"Eisenkot responded"] by accusing him of "relying on a campaign of fear-mongering, lies, and threats—including images of nuclear bombs in the heart of Tel Aviv. This time, it won’t work for him." Trump's endorsement of Netanyahu carries its own political risks a week before a legislative election in which his own Republicans are seeking to hold onto power. The Iran war is deeply unpopular in the United States, blamed for a surge in prices especially for fuel. Major fighting has been suspended for months after ceasefire negotiations held without Israeli participation.

item.title: Anthropic's soaring sales, steep losses put AI frenzy to IPO test
item.description: Anthropic took a big step closer to a potentially record-breaking IPO on Monday, even as it revealed steep losses and security concerns that could test investors' enthusiasm for the AI heavyweight.
item.dc:creator: Manya Saini, Echo Wang
item.content:encoded: Anthropic took a big step closer to a potentially record-breaking IPO on Monday, even as it revealed steep losses and security concerns that could test investors' enthusiasm for the AI heavyweight. AI has captured investors' imagination with the promise of a technological leap that could transform businesses, accelerate scientific breakthroughs and unlock vast productivity gains. That has fueled enormous investments in computing infrastructure and AI development, while also stoking skepticism over the scale and pace of the spending. Anthropic's listing comes at a critical time for global markets as investors closely assess whether the billions of dollars being poured into the technology will generate returns to justify sky-high valuations. "There is still enormous excitement about AI's potential to transform businesses, turbocharge productivity and reshape entire industries, but investors are becoming more discerning," said Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club. Anthropic's net loss in the first half of 2026 [USN:L4N4661JI TEXT:"widened sharply"] to $80.7 billion, largely due to a non-operating item related to bonds convertible into the company's shares. Despite the huge expenses, its operating loss for the same period narrowed to $693 million and its adjusted operating income swung to a positive $1.62 billion compared with a loss of $1.85 billion a year ago. The company, which is expected to go public before Thanksgiving, said its revenue grew a staggering 1,368% in the three months ended June 30 from a year ago, but it warned in the prospectus that its revenue growth rate could decline and fluctuate from time to time. The filing [USN:L4N4500J8 TEXT:"confirmed a series of Reuters "][USN:L4N4500J8 TEXT:"exclusives"] that offered an early peek at its contents before Anthropic made it public, including details of its financial performance, growth trajectory and IPO plans. Its prospectus details the risks from the powerful technology, from potential misuse and security threats to concerns that advanced systems could produce outputs that "could be interpreted as coercive, deceptive, or manipulative", including behavior resembling blackmail. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei [USN:L1N45403P TEXT:"has called for a slowdown"] in the development of AI. VALUATION EXPECTATIONS Some current and prospective investors [USN:L6N4611F6 TEXT:"are valuing Anthropic"] at about $1.5 trillion, down from roughly $2 trillion a week ago, after the AI startup disclosed some financial details at a [USN:L6N4601DE TEXT:"recent investor event"]. "The offering is for the faithful, that sooner or later, they're going to get some return on that invested capital," said Thomas Hayes, chairman at Great Hill Capital. Anthropic's IPO [USN:L6N46216E TEXT:"currently stands alone"] in what was once expected to be a crowded fall listing market. Analysts [USN:L6N46C0UF TEXT:"said"] that would give it access to a deep pool of capital to fund its costly AI ambitions. "Anthropic's IPO will establish a benchmark for valuing leading AI labs, influencing both upcoming listings and confidence in the companies funding the AI infrastructure build-out," IPOX research associate Lukas Muehlbauer said. Analysts expect valuations of the AI sector to correct as [USN:L6N4611C1 TEXT:"investor unease"] with the debt-fueled AI investment boom roils equity and debt markets. Higher borrowing costs and rising bond yields have also added to investor caution. "Anthropic is entering an IPO market that is far more challenging than the summer. Investors were not questioning valuations the same way a few months ago," said Matt Kennedy, senior strategist at Renaissance Capital, a provider of IPO-focused research and ETFs. BALANCING AI'S PROMISES AND PERILS Anthropic said more than half of Fortune 500 companies and over 30% of Global 2000 firms were its customers that generated at least $100,000 each in revenue for the company over the 12 months ended September 30. The IPO comes as Anthropic's own research raises concerns about advanced AI systems, which in controlled tests have shown behaviors including code sabotage, fraud assistance and information manipulation. "Our increasing use of AI systems to accelerate our own research and development may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures," the prospectus said. The company said it relies on a limited number of cloud services providers such as Amazon, Google and Microsoft and suppliers such as Broadcom for compute and critical infrastructure parts. These relationships can create "dependencies and potential vulnerabilities", it said. Anthropic, which [USN:L4N41X0QE TEXT:"did not reveal"] the terms of its offering, will trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT" after the [USN:L4N469189 TEXT:"IPO closes"]. SCORCHING PACE OF GROWTH Anthropic, founded in 2021 by a team of researchers who left OpenAI after disagreements over governance and AI safety, was [USN:L4N4251UW TEXT:"valued at $965 billion"] in a funding round in May. It remains locked in a fierce battle with OpenAI to lead the race to build the most advanced AI systems. The company named Netflix's billionaire co-founder Reed Hastings as its lead independent director. In keeping with Nasdaq rules, Anthropic identified itself as a "controlled company" based on the power of its Long-Term Benefit Trust to elect a majority of its board. The company said it expects compute and infrastructure expenses to rise in absolute dollars and remain its largest operating expense. Anthropic has committed more than $600 billion to computing deals with partners including Amazon and Google, ranking among the largest AI infrastructure commitments on record. Anthropic's IPO follows that of Elon Musk's SpaceX, which rewrote the IPO record books in June, when it [USN:L6N42G18Z TEXT:"priced"] a $75 billion offering that valued the company at $1.75 trillion. Goldman Sachs secured the prestigious lead-left role on Anthropic's IPO, working alongside Morgan Stanley, which is also a lead underwriter. Both banks declined to comment. Twenty other banks were named as underwriters with Morgan Stanley serving as stabilization agent, overseeing the stock's early trading. The IPO mandates mark another win for the two banks, which also held lead roles in SpaceX's IPO.

item.description: SAN FRANCISCO, Oct 26 : Cadence Design Systems on Monday launched a portfolio of AI models tuned to help design computer chips, deepening its open-source model work with Nvidia and diverging from rival Synopsys' recent deal with OpenAI.Both companies make software used to design computing chips — a process

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct 26 : Cadence Design Systems on Monday launched a portfolio of AI models tuned to help design computer chips, deepening its open-source model work with Nvidia and diverging from rival Synopsys' recent deal with OpenAI. Both companies make software used to design computing chips — a process that involves arranging billions of transistors precisely to meet cost and performance targets — and are racing to have AI "agents" use those tools on behalf of human engineers to speed up the process. The new suite, called Cadence Maestro, introduced on Monday, was built in part on Nvidia's open-weight Nemotron model and secured with Nvidia's OpenShell safety technology, the companies said. Cadence said customers can run the models on its own cloud or any public cloud, or keep them entirely in-house behind their own firewalls and data centers.

Shares of Cadence, which reports earnings after market close on Monday, rose 3.9 per cent after the announcement. Customers can also fine-tune the models on their own chip designs, and early results show up to 30 per cent higher quality and up to five times better cost-efficiency than general-purpose models, it added. The Cadence approach contrasts with that of its largest competitor, Synopsys, which on September 30 said it would develop an AI model with OpenAI and share revenue with the ChatGPT maker. That model, GPT-Synopsys, will run on OpenAI-hosted infrastructure. Paul Cunningham, a Cadence senior vice president, framed Maestro as model-agnostic, saying, "there are more (AI) model providers out there than there are (chip design software) vendors." When asked whether Cadence might strike its own deals with proprietary AI labs, Cunningham said both open- and closed-weight approaches were being "pursued equally," and that working with commercial labs was "part of the Maestro vision," though he declined to elaborate. The first Maestro models will reach select early-access customers in the fourth quarter, Cadence said.

item.title: AI gloom revives the specter of stagflation
item.description: AI skittishness has put the brakes on Wall Street's rally, resuscitating demand for US Treasuries as investors seek to protect portfolios, even as surging energy prices stoke inflation. This could put the Federal Reserve in an unenviable stagflationary bind.
item.dc:creator: Jamie McGeever
item.content:encoded: AI skittishness has put the brakes on Wall Street's rally, resuscitating [USN:L4N46803Y TEXT:"demand for US Treasuries"] as investors seek to protect portfolios, even as surging energy prices stoke inflation. This could put the Federal Reserve in an unenviable stagflationary bind. For most of this year, the US bond market has been slammed by an inflation-inducing barrage of soaring energy prices, fiscal fears, and the AI boom. Two of those forces remain very much in play, yet bond yields are no longer on a one-way path higher, with the 10-year falling below 5% for the first time in over a month last Thursday. Investor sentiment around AI is souring. While there has been no single obvious trigger, long-held concerns about the vast sums being spent on the technology have been exacerbated by Big Tech earnings reports detailing gargantuan capital expenditure plans. AI debt markets are wobbling too. While this all may prove to be temporary – just another speed bump in the AI race – the mood shift suggests we may be at the point in the cycle where almost any news is bad news. If so, this should spur a rally in “risk-free” Treasuries. If the AI juggernaut is sputtering, Wall Street and Main Street should sputter too, given how fundamental the technology has become to the stock market and economic growth. But the alarming fiscal outlook hasn't changed, and energy prices are roaring higher again, with US crude futures rising 10% last week to a six-month peak above $110 a barrel, suggesting price pressures and inflation expectations aren't cooling anytime soon. PERSISTENT PRICE PRESSURES A glance at a chart of the 10-year Treasury yield shows how closely correlated energy prices and the bond market have been this year. The 10-year yield's lowest daily close in 2026 was 3.96% on Friday, February 27, the day before the US and Israel attacked Iran. The subsequent surge in global crude, gas and fuel prices then propelled Treasury yields to their highest levels in more than two decades as investors bet that inflationary pressures would intensify. The 10-year yield reached 5.36% earlier this month. But that relationship has broken down recently. Oil prices eased for a few weeks beginning in mid-September, but the relentless rise in bond yields continued. Now oil prices have rebounded sharply, yet Treasury yields are in retreat, culminating in last Thursday's steep decline of 20 basis points. Typically, a global energy shock would be expected to slow economic growth, causing investors to flee to the Treasury market. However, for most of this year, the tailwind from the AI juggernaut has kept the economy and Wall Street humming. If the AI narrative is turning, bond investors will have to consider the potential valuation destruction and economic fallout from a deflating AI bubble. That appears to be offsetting any fears of "higher-for-longer" energy prices. But the move back toward Treasuries may not be a simple switch to flick. 'STAGFLATION' RETURN? That’s because "stagflation" could return to investors' lexicon. A mix of stagnant growth and sticky inflation would complicate life for the Federal Open Market Committee. While it raised its policy rate in September, it will almost certainly keep it on hold this Wednesday ahead of next week's midterm elections. Markets still expect it to tighten again in the coming months, but that assumes inflationary pressures outweigh AI wobbles. Last week, one-year market-based inflation expectations climbed to 2.80%, as measured by inflation swaps. That’s the highest since June, though the rise in longer-dated inflation swap rates has been less dramatic, suggesting investors don't believe the energy shock will become deeply embedded in higher goods and services prices. Fed policymakers will likely be banking on that. But it's a risky bet. Producer prices, often a leading indicator of consumer prices, are rising at the fastest pace in four years. The gap between producer and consumer price inflation is also the widest in four years. And it's worth repeating that consumer price inflation has been above the Fed's 2% target for close to six years. "All main inflation measures are expected to increase over the next couple of months as base effects from last year's government shutdown in October and November create a low bar for rising inflation," UBS economists say. "We expect little easing in inflation before the spring of next year," when the base effects from the start of the Iran war kick in. Can the Fed afford to "look through" the latest spike in energy prices, while hoping that the AI wobbles don't snowball? (The opinions expressed here are those of the author, a columnist for Reuters) Enjoying this column? Check out Reuters Open Interest (ROI), your essential new source for global financial commentary. Follow ROI on LinkedIn, and X. And listen to the Morning Bid daily podcast on Apple, Spotify, or the Reuters app. Subscribe to hear Reuters journalists discuss the biggest news in markets and finance seven days a week.

item.title: Serbia's new leaders face host of tough challenges
item.description: Serbia's student-led protest movement won a historic victory in Sunday's parliamentary election, ending the long rule of Aleksandar Vucic and sparking mass celebrations. But their yet-to-be named leaders face a long list of issues.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Serbia's student-led protest movement [USN:L6N46B017 TEXT:"won a historic victory"] in Sunday's parliamentary election, ending the long rule of Aleksandar Vucic and sparking mass celebrations. But their yet-to-be named [USN:L8N4650K6 TEXT:"leaders"] face a long list of issues. Here are a few of them: KOSOVO The Student List believes that Kosovo, which declared independence from Belgrade in 2008, remains an integral part of Serbia. During their campaign, the students' candidates said that Kosovo is a temporarily occupied territory which could be reintegrated into Serbia through peaceful means, diplomacy and dialogue. Their focus is preventing the exodus of the Serbian population in the north of Kosovo, and strengthening institutions funded by Serbia and operating under the Serbian legal system, such as healthcare and education. They want Kosovo's Serb communities to operate autonomously, rejecting previous agreements with the ethnic Albanian-led government in Pristina, such as those on energy, vehicle licence plates and the use of the dinar currency. FRAYED EU RELATIONS With Serbia's European Union accession talks largely stalled by a lack of necessary reforms, the Student List campaign deliberately avoided such polarising foreign policy issues. Prominent candidates, including former central bank governor Dejan Soskic and cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, have said the government must first focus on domestic reforms and close all EU negotiating clusters before asking the public to cast a definitive ballot on membership of the bloc. The Student List position on Kosovo is also at odds with membership of the EU, which requires Belgrade to normalise relations with Pristina. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the bloc [USN:L6N46B0AC TEXT:"stood ready to support reforms"] including on the rule of law and media freedom, and to work together to advance Serbia’s future in the EU. COMPLEX RUSSIAN RELATIONSHIP AND US SANCTIONS AGAINST NIS OIL FIRM The Student List must navigate an intricate energy and foreign policy web with traditional Serbian ally Russia. The students have said they have no plans to align with the EU and impose sanctions on Moscow over its war in Ukraine. The new government would be reliant on US sanctions waivers to maintain crude imports while it waits for the [USN:L1N45M0TB TEXT:"sale of Russia's stake"] in energy company NIS (NIIS.BEL) , which operates Serbia's only oil refinery, to Hungary’s MOL (MOLB.BU) . Russia's Gazprom (GAZP.MM) is also Serbia’s biggest gas supplier, delivering around 2.2 billion cubic meters a year at below-market pricing. The Student List said this energy reliance was not a geopolitical alignment, but an acute economic dependency. The Student List's top candidates had not said whether a future government would end all arms exports from Serbia to war zones, including sales to Western intermediaries who pass weapons to Ukraine. Vucic cultivated strong personal ties with both Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy and Russian President Vladimir Putin. CORRUPTION The Student List’s anti-corruption program centres on institutional overhauls, such as the creation of an independent police unit accountable to prosecutors rather than the Interior Ministry and a purge of police officers linked to organised crime or violent crackdowns on protests. They want a ban on the appointments of party loyalists to state-owned companies in favour of transparent, merit-based hiring. Financial accountability and fiscal oversight would include a strict asset origin law allowing the state to audit, seize and return illegally acquired wealth from officials to the state budget. Convicted officials would be barred from holding public office. The students' anti-corruption program also envisions public scrutiny of all major state infrastructure contracts and the creation of independent oversight bodies to curb the misuse of public funds. Vucic, the SNS and the authorities repeatedly denied accusations of repression and corruption. ECONOMY Serbia's economy is deeply integrated with both the European market and international investment flows. The IMF has forecast Serbia's economic growth at 3% in 2026 and 4% in 2027. Inflation in September stood at 4.1%, almost double August's 2.2%, while the central bank has maintained a 5.75% benchmark rate since 2024. The Student List’s economic platform shifts Serbia’s growth model away from state-backed infrastructure projects and cheap labour to domestic market security and labour rights. Central to the plan is a campaign against retail monopolies to lower food prices, coupled with a tax overhaul that raises levies on wealthy citizens and cuts them for lower-income groups. The movement has pledged to sharply lower the maximum allowed duration for temporary work. Fiscal sustainability would rely heavily on anti-corruption savings and rigorous state oversight. Social spending would be focused on curbing a youth exodus through an affordable housing initiative for young couples, teachers and healthcare staff, alongside guaranteeing free school textbooks and cheaper, state-subsidised medication. (This story has been corrected to say top student leaders had not said whether a future government would halt weapons exports, in paragraph 15.)

item.title: In China, the AI bubble has already burst
item.description: While global tech stocks teeter, in China they have already crashed as lofty valuations collapse under worries about AI demand and curbs on Chinese exports.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: While global tech stocks teeter, in China they have already crashed as lofty valuations collapse under worries about AI demand and curbs on Chinese exports. The meltdown, tanking the mainland STAR50 index (.STAR50) of AI and semiconductor leaders by 40% in less than four months and vaporising some $480 billion in market value, is an ill omen for wobbly world markets and a dampener on China's efforts at encouraging its savers into stocks to fund the AI boom. It has also slammed the brakes on a rally running two years, since economic stimulus promises sent shares soaring, and has stalled Beijing's push to break with a long boom-bust pattern and drive a "slow bull" market that delivers reliable performance. China's broad blue-chip index (.CSI300) has dropped about 20% from highs made in June. "The stock market later evolved into a speculative crazy bull," said Beijing-based fund manager Dong Baozhen. "And now we see the bubble bursting." The reversal reflects a rally that ran to higher heights than markets in the West or elsewhere in Asia, and compares with a mere prick to US AI stocks, which have led a 6% drawdown in the Nasdaq (.IXIC) from a record high scaled three weeks ago. There has been no obvious selling trigger in China, although traders said high prices, tax bills and the threat of the US or other nations banning Chinese equipment in data centres all contributed. With AI stocks running to 42% of China's market capitalisation and 57% of turnover across mainland-listed A-shares and Hong Kong's H-shares, according to Goldman Sachs, few in a market dominated by small investors have escaped pain. RETAIL FAVOURITES SLIDE Shares in robot-maker Unitree (688836.SS) , 8,000 times oversubscribed by retail buyers at listing, have halved since they started trading in August, and chipmaker CXMT (688825.SS) has lost more than a quarter of its value in the past month. Chipmakers MetaX Integrated Circuits (688802.SS) and Moore Threads Technology (688795.SS) , which leapt 700% and 400% respectively on their market debuts last year, have also halved in value since July. Chen Wensheng, a small business owner and investor from China's southern Hainan, said he bought into the rally emboldened by what he felt was official support for the likes of Unitree, which counted state-backed funds as investors. But Chen and his friends are now nursing losses. Frustration that an investment theme backed by Beijing has ended so badly has driven many investors into defensive assets and is likely to slow equity fundraising by tech firms. Shares in optical parts makers Zhongji Innolight (300308.SZ) and Eoptolink Technology (300502.SZ) are down roughly 60% from highs in June and July, in part as Washington moves towards banning the one-time darlings from supplying US data centres. With the STAR50 index still at around 100 times trailing earnings, albeit down from a high of nearly 250, investors compare the Nasdaq 100's multiple of 30 and worry the selloff could get worse before it gets better. "What's happening is now going to put a stop for many of the companies trying to get themselves listed," said Hong Hao, managing partner and chief investment officer at Lotus Asset Management in Hong Kong. 'ALL BUBBLES INEVITABLY BURST' The frenzy and its [USN:L4N3YY09D TEXT:"fallout"] contrast with a push by authorities to improve returns and dampen volatility by cracking down on leverage and high-frequency trading. State-backed investors were sellers into rallies to keep gains in check. China's market regulator, the China Securities Regulatory Commission, did not immediately reply to questions faxed by Reuters last week. CRSC Chairman Wu Qing met with market participants earlier this month to hear suggestions on improving capital markets, the regulator said on its website, and some in the investment community say the boom has been bad for the market's structure. "Overemphasising the 'technology content' — that is, the weighting of tech companies by market value in major indexes — leads to a deviation, even a distortion, in capital behaviour," said Leo Wang, partner at Beijing-based Qianchuang Capital. "This created a severe bubble in certain sectors and a serious drain on others." Some see value in the selloff, saying it is neither surprising nor detrimental to market reforms that are geared for the long term and have gained traction in driving up returns, particularly income, in recent years. Although they have been sellers over the past three months, Asia funds in general are overweight on China, according to HSBC research. Goldman Sachs has Innolight and CXMT among dozens of Chinese AI stocks on a revamped recommendation list it published earlier this month, and BNP Paribas Securities strategist William Bratton has said the market offers buying opportunities for the careful. Still, on the mainland many are looking at other sectors or for even lower valuations before they turn buyers. "Just like all other Chinese manufacturers, (chipmakers and AI suppliers) will eventually end up in a price war," said fund manager Wang Zhuo, partner at Shanghai Zhuozhu Investment Management. "There's no exception," he said. "All bubbles inevitably burst."

item.title: Ambani, Adani outlets among Indian publishers contesting Modi’s privacy law
item.description: A group of 21 news publishers, including companies owned by billionaires Mukesh Ambani and Gautam Adani, has challenged India's privacy law in court, arguing it would trample investigative work and let New Delhi identify journalists' sources, documents show.
item.dc:creator: Aditya Kalra
item.content:encoded: A group of 21 news publishers, including companies owned by billionaires Mukesh Ambani and Gautam Adani, has challenged India's privacy law in court, arguing it would trample investigative work and let New Delhi identify journalists' sources, documents show. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government last year announced implementation of a privacy law to [USN:L4N3WQ0V8 TEXT:"protect digital personal data"] of users, raising compliance requirements for platforms like Meta and Google. The publishers have said that since media outlets were not exempt, the law was an invasion of press freedom. Media companies received assurances in an August meeting with the government that the law would protect press freedom, but not having a written carve-out for journalists like in the European Union, Singapore and Britain was alarming, India's Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA) said in a confidential filing at the Supreme Court, reviewed by Reuters. The October 6 lawsuit, being reported for the first time and due to be heard on Tuesday, is the most high-profile challenge to Modi’s privacy law. Until now, only free speech activists and a group of smaller news outlets had [USN:L4N3ZZ10J TEXT:"challenged"] it. It also marks an unusual challenge to the government from businesses headed by Ambani and Adani, who opposition parties allege are close to Modi and get favourable treatment - charges the businesses and the government vehemently deny. DNPA and the media groups did not respond to requests for comment from Reuters, and neither did India's information technology ministry. The publishers are demanding that most of the law's contentious provisions, which kick in from May 2027, should be quashed. They are arguing the law could force a journalist to get prior consent from a person they want to investigate and force publishers to erase stories. They also say powers granted by the law to demand information could expose reporters' sources. The law would "render investigative journalism a benign and neutered recorder of events," the 698-page filing said. The provisions "constitute pre-censorship which is anathema to any democracy worth its name". The lawsuit comes amid accusations of declining press freedom in India since Modi took office in 2014. Critics say many mainstream media outlets have [USN:L4N43Q0BR TEXT:"not done enough"] to scrutinise Modi’s government. India's ranking in Reporters Without Borders’ World Press Freedom Index fell to 157th out of 180 countries this year, from 140th in 2014 - but the government rejects the rankings. Modi's government says it respects press freedom and says India, which has a "vibrant press and media ecosystem" of hundreds of newspapers and TV channels, does not need validation from foreign bodies. CONCERNS OVER CONSENT DNPA's members include Ambani's Network18, which has seven digital news platforms, Adani's NDTV (NDTV.NS) and other marquee media groups including the Indian Express and Times Internet, which is part of the Times of India group, publisher of India's largest-selling English-language daily. A key concern in the law is the requirement of consent, the group's filing says. A social media platform or online retailer can seek consent from users when they sign up, but the DNPA has argued that requiring a journalist to notify the subject of an investigation and seek consent "would allow that subject to destroy evidence, intimidate witnesses". The law also lets people withdraw consent at any time and demand that their data be erased, without any public-interest safeguard, which DNPA says could force its members to unpublish or heavily redact a factual news report. FEAR OF SOURCES AT RISK News publishers are concerned that a federal authority created under the law can impose fines for non-compliance, and grants powers to New Delhi to block access to any information in the "interests of the general public", which would curtail press freedom, DNPA said. In an August letter to the government attached to the lawsuit, the group said India "has chosen to grant broad exemptions to the state, while failing to extend any corresponding protection to the press". No response was cited. From next year, the law will also let New Delhi order any organization handling personal data “to furnish such information as it may call for”, putting newsrooms at risk of having to divulge sources, the filing said. It can also deter whistleblowers from sharing information on corruption, corporate wrongdoing or electoral malpractice with reporters, the DNPA argued. The “nakedly unguided” provision must be quashed, the DNPA said, adding that the power “can extend to privileged communications in possession of a reporter or the informant.”

item.title: Equities end higher as Anthropic's IPO filing buoys AI stocks
item.description: US stocks closed higher on Monday, with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq coming off consecutive weekly declines, as Anthropic's IPO filing helped boost sentiment in AI-related stocks in a week filled with a host of market catalysts.
item.dc:creator: Chuck Mikolajczak, Shashwat Chauhan
item.content:encoded: US stocks closed higher on Monday, with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq coming off consecutive weekly declines, as Anthropic's IPO filing helped boost sentiment in AI-related stocks in a week filled with a host of market catalysts. [USN:L3N46C10M TEXT:"Anthropic disclosed"] steep losses and red-hot revenue growth in its filing for a US initial public offering, laying out its ambition to build AI systems capable of reshaping the global economy despite the high costs of developing the technology. The AI lab is pushing ahead with its listing plans even as a once-lively autumn IPO calendar has slowed, with recent market volatility prompting companies to delay offerings. Anthropic's filing comes as investors increasingly dissect the potential payoff from massive AI spending and at the start of an eventful week. On tap are the Federal Reserve's policy statement on Wednesday, readings on economic growth and inflation on Thursday and a slew of corporate earnings reports throughout the week. More than a third of S&P 500 companies are scheduled to report earnings this week, including hyperscalers Alphabet (GOOGL.O) , Microsoft (MSFT.O) and Amazon.com (AMZN.O) , whose results will be [USN:L6N45T17Q TEXT:"parsed for signs"] of whether the hefty AI investments are translating into growth. "Today's all about the Anthropic release, so we're back on a little bit of an optimistic tilt, I would say. But there's a lot in that release. It will be interesting to see how well things are received when they actually come to list," said JP Powers, chief investment officer at RWA Wealth Partners in Boston. "The risk is maybe a little bit of a whipsaw if things aren't all moving in the same direction. A little optimism today, but who knows what will happen from some of these other releases this week," he said. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) rose 146.42 points, or 0.28%, to 52,361.58, the S&P 500 (.SPX) gained 53.09 points, or 0.70%, to 7,676.77 and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) gained 214.04 points, or 0.83%, to 26,169.38. Semiconductor and chip-related companies, widely viewed as some of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom, helped fuel the gains. The broader Philadelphia chips index (.SOX) was up 2.8% on the day but is still down 12.2% on the month. Meta shares closed down 1.9% after the social media company said it [USN:L3N46C0RT TEXT:"plans to raise"] up to $95 billion in equity to fund its AI-related expansion of data centers, cloud computing power and other infrastructure. The AI trade has come under pressure this month amid concerns that debt-funded spending may become harder to justify in the face of climbing borrowing costs. The Anthropic filing helped buoy sentiment, however, as neocloud firms, including CoreWeave (CRWV.O) , erased earlier declines. Other AI-linked companies, including photonic product makers Lumentum (LITE.O) and Coherent (COHR.N) , were among the best-performing S&P 500 stocks. Lumentum and Coherent gained about 8% and 6%, respectively. The technology index (.SPLRCT) led gains among the 11 major S&P 500 sectors, climbing 1.5%. Megacap and growth stocks were also mostly higher. Tesla (TSLA.O) jumped 5.2% to close at its highest level in more than three months after Barclays upgraded its rating on the stock to "overweight" from "equal-weight." Markets are pricing in only a 12.7% chance of a rate hike from the Fed on Wednesday, according to CME FedWatch. But with inflation pressures showing no signs of abating, market [USN:L6N46518P TEXT:"participants do not believe"] the central bank will be on hold for long. Investors are also bracing for the November 3 midterm elections , which will decide control of the US Congress. Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.36-to-1 ratio on the New York Stock Exchange and by a 1.09-to-1 ratio on the Nasdaq. The S&P 500 posted seven new 52-week highs and seven new lows, while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 82 new highs and 349 new lows. Volume on US exchanges was 16.7 billion shares, compared with the 17.2 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days.

item.title: Officials from Mecca pact countries to meet Iranian officials in Tehran
item.description: This will be the first high-level contact between Iran and all members of the three-nation bloc since Saudi Arabia was drawn deeper into the wider Iran conflict.
item.dc:creator: CNA
item.content:encoded:
Advertisement

World

Officials from Mecca pact countries to meet Iranian officials in Tehran

This will be the first high-level contact between Iran and all members of the three-nation bloc since Saudi Arabia was drawn deeper into the wider Iran conflict.

Mecca defence pact meeting between Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, Oct 5, 2026. (Photo: REUTERS/Saudi Press Agency)

26 Oct 2026 05:45PM

Bookmark

Bookmark

Share

Set CNA as your preferred source on Google

Click here to return to FAST Tap here to return to FAST

FAST

Top officials from Mecca Pact countries Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan are to meet Iran's leaders in Tehran on Monday (Oct 26) in their first high-level contact since the kingdom became a pressure point in the wider Iran conflict.

Saudi Arabia will be represented by Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan by army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Turkiye by intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin, Saudi and Iranian officials said.

Attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have spiralled in recent weeks and rhetoric between Washington and Tehran has grown more heated. Both countries have also drawn up plans to restart the wider war, possibly after the US midterm elections on Nov 3.

Monday's planned talks will be the first high-level contact between Iran and all members of the three-nation bloc since Saudi Arabia was drawn deeper into the conflict. Under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed in August, an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday discussions on regional security would include "Israel’s expansionist policies, developments in the Palestinian territories and Lebanon, and the repercussions of US and Israeli military action against Iran."

Baghaei said the meeting, proposed during a visit by Munir to Tehran last week, could be a first step towards establishing regional security mechanisms based on the interests of countries in the region.

Related:

CNA Explains: What is the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement?

Commentary: How far will Pakistan go in defending Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks?

(From left) Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, and Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif pose after signing a joint defence agreement in Mecca, Saudi Arabia on Aug 7, 2026. (Photo: Saudi Press Agency/Handout via Reuters)

Qatari mediators met Iranian officials in Tehran on Sunday in a push to de-escalate regional tensions, Reuters reported. Qatar has, for months, played a mediating role between Tehran and Washington.

A senior Iranian official said the meeting was initiated by Pakistan, during Munir's visit to Tehran, as he met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and other senior officials. During the visit, Iranian officials told him there would be no talks with Washington until Tehran's demands were met, according to Iranian media.

Earlier mediation efforts involving both Pakistan and Qatar helped produce an interim peace agreement in June, but the deal quickly unravelled as fighting between Iran and the United States resumed weeks later.

The deputy secretary of Iran's top security body, Ali Baqeri-Kani, told state TV that Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid, Pakistan's Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin would visit Tehran for consultations with Iran’s Supreme National Security Council on regional security.

Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Rayed Krimly said the meeting is part of ongoing efforts by the Mecca Pact countries to de-escalate the current crisis, promote diplomatic solutions, and support mediation efforts led by Qatar and Pakistan.

"The visit also underscores the pivotal role of the Mecca Pact states in fostering regional security and stability, and their commitment to working with all nations in the region toward achieving this goal," Krimly posted on X.

Pakistan's military media wing and Turkiye's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Related:

UK to deploy fighter jets to help protect Saudi from Houthi attacks

Türkiye sending technical, defensive support to Saudi Arabia to help fight Houthis, officials say

TENSIONS RISING Saudi Arabia intercepted another wave of missiles and drones on Sunday as fighting with the Houthis continued unabated. Ministers from the Mecca Pact countries held an emergency meeting in Riyadh earlier this month and agreed to ensure the "rapid deployment" of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.

The Houthi attacks have become an increasingly destabilising element in the US-Israeli conflict with Iran, turning US ally Saudi Arabia into a pressure point in the wider war.

Tensions between Washington and Tehran have sharpened in recent days. President Donald Trump said on Friday the US may carry out another military operation against Iran and Iran's leaders have said that a renewed US military campaign would be met with a stronger response than before.

Iranian security officials have told Reuters that Tehran has drawn up detailed plans to hit Gulf undersea cables if the United States and Israel attack again. A US intelligence memo this week warned that Iranian plots against American personnel had reached "advanced stages".

The war, now nearly eight months old, has weighed on President Donald Trump's approval ratings ahead of the midterms.

The Mecca agreement's first article says the parties shall use "all necessary means" to eliminate threats to one another's territorial integrity, sovereignty or internationally recognised borders, according to a text seen by Reuters.

Efforts by Turkiye’s parliament to ratify the agreement began last week and are still underway, while Pakistan approved the pact last week.

Source: Reuters/ia

item.title: Trump says Brazil election looked 'rigged,' defeated Bolsonaro's party recognizes Lula win
item.description: "I didn't take sides, but it looked like another rigged election," Trump told reporters, without providing any evidence. "It looked very bad to me."
item.dc:creator: Oliver Griffin, Eduardo Simões
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump said on Monday that leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's surprise win in [USN:L2N46B01X TEXT:"Brazil's presidential vote"] "looked like another rigged election," although the party of defeated right-winger Flavio Bolsonaro later acknowledged the result. The son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat in [USN:L2N46B01X TEXT:"Sunday's presidential election"], saying he would seek the annulment of Lula's victory after the Supreme Court extended voting by two hours. Later on Monday, however, Bolsonaro's Liberal Party said it [USN:S0N46906S TEXT:"acknowledged the runoff result"] in a statement signed by the party's head Valdemar Costa Neto. "We recognize the presidential election results," Costa Neto said. "But we believe the issues raised need to be properly clarified." Bolsonaro, who has not commented publicly since his party's statement, said earlier on Monday he would comply with a federal police order to hand over his passports following a visit to his father, who is under house arrest, and denied he was planning to flee Brazil. Trump did not endorse Bolsonaro ahead of the vote, although Reuters has reported that officials from his State Department [USN:L1N4650X8 TEXT:"led a campaign"] to return the Bolsonaros to power. "I didn't take sides, but it looked like another rigged election," Trump told reporters, without providing any evidence. "It looked very bad to me." Bolsonaro lost to Lula by over 4 million votes, a clear result that it will be challenging for him to overturn. Fewer than 35,000 votes, or some 0.03% of the total, were cast in the extra two hours of voting ordered by the Supreme Court, according to an analysis of electoral records by Insper professor Pedro Burgos. "I just think it had a very bad look, the election, the way it was tabulated," Trump said. "The extension given was very strange." Vice President Geraldo Alckmin later defended Brazil's electoral system, saying in a TV interview with Rede Vanguarda that Trump's remarks were "totally wrong" and "unfounded." Neither Trump nor Jair Bolsonaro accepted their election losses in 2020 and 2022, respectively. Brazil's former president was handed a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing to Lula. Analysts do not expect Flavio Bolsonaro to be able to build the same anti-democratic movement as his father in 2022. MARKETS ROILED BY LULA WIN World leaders have already widely congratulated Lula on his unprecedented fourth mandate, which was greeted with [USN:L2N46C051 TEXT:"dismay by investors"] who had been betting on a Bolsonaro win. Brazil's real fell 8.1% against the dollar in its biggest one-day drop since 2002, while the stock exchange marked its steepest one-day fall since 2020. "The initial selloff could moderate as election-related positions are unwound, but investors will demand convincing fiscal commitments before rebuilding exposure," said Pantheon Macroeconomics' chief Latin America economist Andres Abadia. Lula's victory defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America. He trailed Bolsonaro in the first round, but managed to convince voters to come out for him in the runoff. Pollsters said a higher-than-expected turnout and an improved [USN:L6N46815Z TEXT:"social media campaign"] helped power Lula to victory. During the campaign, Lula pointed to his track record of cutting poverty and inequality while also highlighting record-low unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation, but his fourth term may prove challenging. He will face an [USN:L6N46B06R TEXT:"uphill battle"] for his agenda in a Congress [USN:L6N45R137 TEXT:"packed with Bolsonaro allies"] after a surge of conservative voters in the first round of the general election pushed the Brazilian legislature further to the right.

item.title: Jordan arrests three suspects in deadly church attack
item.description: Gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church on Friday, killing nine people and wounding 40 others.
item.dc:creator: CNA
item.content:encoded:
Advertisement

World

Jordan arrests three suspects in deadly church attack

Gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church on Friday, killing nine people and wounding 40 others.

A hearse with the coffin of a victim of a church shooting, in Karak, Jordan, October 25, 2026. REUTERS/Alaa Al Sukhni

26 Oct 2026 02:14PM

Get bite-sized news via a new cards interface. Give it a try.

Click here to return to FAST Tap here to return to FAST

FAST

Jordanian security forces have arrested three suspects in connection with an attack on a church in the US-allied country that killed nine people, state television reported on Monday (Oct 26).  The attack, in which gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church on Friday in the village of Hamoud in Karak governorate, about 120 km southwest of the capital Amman, also wounded 40 others. The shooting lasted several minutes, witnesses said. Jordan's Public Security Directorate said security forces located the three suspects early on Monday hiding in an abandoned house in Karak. The suspects refused to surrender and opened fire on security forces, who returned fire and arrested all three after they were wounded, the directorate said in a statement carried on state media. No security personnel were injured, and a number of firearms and ammunition were found in the suspects' possession after their arrest. "Terrorism has no place among us," the directorate said, adding that the suspects had met their "just fate". The Public Security Directorate did not identify the suspects' affiliation or say whether they belonged to any militant group.

The grounds of Saint George’s Greek Orthodox Church, where gunmen opened fire during a funeral the previous day, is cordoned-off, in the village of Hamoud, Karak, Jordan, October 24, 2026. REUTERS/Alaa Al Sukhni

Jordanian authorities have said the attack was carried out by "extremist terrorists", but it was too early to determine whether they had links to known groups inside or outside Jordan. There has been no claim of responsibility. Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya said on Monday authorities were reviewing the circumstances that led young people towards extremism and would hold accountable anyone found to have participated in the attack. King Abdullah, a US partner in the fight against Islamist militant groups, has ordered security forces to respond with an "iron fist" to the rare attack on Jordan's Christian minority. Such violence is highly unusual in Jordan, a relatively stable state in the Middle East, though authorities say they have foiled several Islamist militant plots over the years.

Related:

Singapore leaders condemn deadly church attack in Jordan, convey condolences to victims' families

Source: Reuters/aj
